1149.title: The highest rung
1149.hook: a loan, a partnership or a job, so the person needn't ask again
1149.carry: so they never need to ask
1149.howItsDone: Jewish communities run interest-free loan funds, each called a gemach, and Hebrew Free Loan societies, along with job and business help, as ways of giving at the highest rung.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maimonides' ladder of giving, from the grudging gift to the open hand. Your line: the eight rungs. Today, the top.

A heavy load starts to slip off a donkey's back. One person walking alongside can reach up and steady it. Wait until it crashes to the ground, and even a group will struggle to lift it back. That picture comes from Rashi, drawing on older teaching, in his commentary on a verse in Leviticus about a brother starting to fall into poverty. Catch it early. Maimonides builds the top of his ladder on that same verse.
screen: `A LOAD BEGINS TO SLIP.` → `ONE PERSON CAN STEADY IT.` → `ONCE IT FALLS, IT'S HARD TO LIFT.`

segments.voice: The highest rung. In plain English: the greatest level, above which there is none, is to strengthen the hand of someone who has become poor. Give them a gift or a loan, go into partnership with them, or find them work, until they don't need to ask anyone. First, the verse. Leviticus says, when your brother grows poor and his hand falters beside you, uphold him. In Hebrew, v'hechezakta bo: strengthen him, hold him firm. Maimonides echoes it: strengthen their hand. Second, the list. A gift, yes. But also a loan, which comes back. A partnership, where both stand to gain. A job. None of these looks much like charity, and some might even look like business. He puts them at the top. Third, the aim. Every lower rung relieves a need. This one ends it. The goal is not that the person feels grateful to you, but that they no longer need you, or anyone. Fourth, the timing. Remember the donkey. The verse speaks of a hand only beginning to falter. The highest rung often comes before the fall: the loan that keeps a shop open, the introduction that lands someone work, the partner who shares the risk. It can look ordinary. It might not feel like giving at all. That may be part of why it sits so high. The person helped keeps their dignity, and walks on.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose hand is faltering a little: a friend looking for work, a neighbor learning something new, a younger colleague. Ask gently what would strengthen their hand rather than carry them, an introduction, a skill you could teach, a reference, and let one concrete step become clear.
The highest rung. In Maimonides' ladder, strengthening someone with a gift, a loan, a partnership or a job, so they won't need to ask anyone. Today's word.
Your line: so they never need to ask. At this height, a good gift works itself out of a job. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1150.title: Neither knows: the chamber of secrets
1150.hook: giving where giver and receiver don't know each other
1150.carry: neither knows: a gift for its own sake
1150.howItsDone: Jews give through community charity funds and collection boxes, called pushkes in Yiddish, so that the giver and the receiver need not know each other.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the top of the ladder: a loan, a partner, a job, so they never need to ask. Today, one rung down, and a quiet room.

In the Temple in Jerusalem, Maimonides writes, there was a room called the chamber of secrets. Righteous people would go in quietly and leave something. Poor people from good families were supported from it, just as quietly. The giver never saw who took. The one who took never saw who gave. Maimonides points to that room when he describes the rung just below the top of his ladder.
screen: `THE CHAMBER OF SECRETS.` → `GIVERS GO IN QUIETLY.` → `RECEIVERS GO IN QUIETLY.`

segments.voice: Neither knows. The rung, in plain English: below the highest is one who gives to the poor without knowing to whom he gives, while the poor person doesn't know from whom he takes. Maimonides calls this doing the commandment for its own sake. First, what disappears. The giver gets no thanks, no nod at synagogue, no quiet feeling of being owed. The receiver owes nobody: no awkward meeting in the market, no lowering of the eyes. Second, for its own sake. Lishmah, in Hebrew. With every reward stripped away, what's left is the gift itself. No one can give to be seen when no one can see. Third, the room today. Something close to this rung, he says, is giving into the community's charity fund, but only if the person in charge is trustworthy, wise, and knows how to manage it properly. Anonymous giving depends on an honest middle. Without one, the secret room is just a dark room. Fourth, why it's not the top. The highest rung is personal: a loan, a job, a partnership, help that ends the need. Neither knows relieves need rather than ending it. One protects dignity by hiding the giver. The other protects it by making the gift unnecessary. A community needs both kinds of room: the quiet chamber, and the open door to work.

segments.voice: Think of a way to give where your name stays out of it: a trusted fund, an unsigned gift, paying for something no one will trace back to you. Then notice what part of you wants to be known for it, even a little. Don't fight it; just see it, and let it sit beside the gift.

1151.title: Teshuvah: the path of return
1151.hook: teshuvah: recognize, regret, confess, resolve; read in full next year
1151.carry: teshuvah: recognize, regret, confess, resolve, repair
1151.howItsDone: Jews practice teshuvah all year, and especially in the month of Elul and the Days of Awe before Yom Kippur, when it is customary to seek forgiveness from people one has wronged before asking it of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chamber of secrets, where giver and receiver never meet. Your line: neither knows: a gift for its own sake. Today, the road that closes the Book of Knowledge.

"O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God." The prophet Hosea calls it out, and his word, return, runs through Jewish prayer. Tradition reads Hosea's call on the Shabbat between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and names that Shabbat for it. And return is the subject Maimonides chose to close his Book of Knowledge. Back on day nineteen, you met teshuvah as return, not repentance. Today, the steps of the road.
screen: `RETURN UNTO THE LORD THY GOD.` → `A WORD ALL THROUGH JEWISH LIFE.` → `THE BOOK OF KNOWLEDGE ENDS HERE.`

segments.voice: The path of return. Teshuvah: less repentance than turning around, coming back. Maimonides asks plainly what teshuvah is, and answers with steps. First, recognize and leave. The person stops doing the wrong thing, and takes it out of their thoughts. You can't turn from a road you won't admit you're on. Second, regret. Not a passing wince, but real sorrow, looking back. Third, confess. The person puts it into words, out loud. At the very start of these laws, he describes those words: I did this, I am sorry, I am ashamed, I will not do it again. Spoken, not only felt. Fourth, resolve: never to return to that act. And he adds a striking test: the One who knows all hidden things can bear witness that this person won't go back. The resolve has to be real all the way down. Then one more line, which matters a great deal. For wrongs done to another person, turning to God is not enough. A person must repair what was harmed, and seek the other person's forgiveness. The path of return runs through the people we hurt. Next year, this path reads these laws in full. Today, just the outline of the road: recognize, regret, confess, resolve.
screen: `RECOGNIZE AND LEAVE IT.` · `REGRET WHAT WAS DONE.` · `SAY IT ALOUD.` · `RESOLVE NOT TO RETURN.` · then, large: `THE PATH OF RETURN.`

segments.voice: Let one small, true thing come to mind that you'd like to turn from: a sharp tone, a shortcut, a silence where you owed a word. Recognize it, and notice whatever regret is there, without drowning in it. If it's safe and private, say it once, quietly, in plain words, then picture the next time it comes up, and see yourself turning the other way.
The path of return. Teshuvah: in Maimonides' laws, recognizing and leaving a wrong, regretting it, saying it aloud, and resolving not to go back. Today's word.
Your line: teshuvah: recognize, regret, confess, resolve, repair. Four steps, one road home, and it runs through the people we hurt. Same time tomorrow.

1152.title: You can be Moses (Teshuvah 5:2)
1152.hook: every person can become righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam
1152.howItsDone: Some Jews study the Mishneh Torah's Laws of Repentance, including chapter five on free choice, in the season before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, when return is the theme.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the path of return: recognize, regret, confess, resolve. Today, the question underneath it: can a person really change?

Two names sit side by side in a law book. One is Moses, who stood on the mountain and brought down the Torah. The other is Jeroboam, a king of Israel who set up golden calves and led people away. You might expect a writer to put them at opposite ends of the universe, made of different stuff. Maimonides does something stranger. In the middle of his laws of return, he puts the two names in the same sentence, and he puts you between them. Either one, he says, is open to you.
screen: `MOSES ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `JEROBOAM AND THE CALVES.` → `AND YOU, BETWEEN THEM.`

segments.voice: You can be Moses. It's from the fifth chapter of the Laws of Repentance in the Mishneh Torah. First, the claim. Permission is given to every human being, Maimonides writes. Want to turn toward the good way and be righteous? You can. Toward the bad way? You can. Every person can be righteous like Moses our teacher, or wicked like Jeroboam. Wise or foolish, merciful or cruel. Second, what he's pushing against. He calls foolish the idea that God decrees at birth whether a person will be righteous or wicked. Nobody forces a person, nobody decrees it, nobody drags them down either road. The person chooses. Third, why it sits here. If your character were fixed at birth, regret would be pointless and resolve would be theater. Return only works if the road can change direction. He calls this freedom a great principle, a pillar of the Torah and the commandments, and grounds it in Deuteronomy, where life and good, death and evil, are set before the people, and the call comes: "therefore choose life." Fourth, the hard part. If God knows everything ahead of time, how can a person really choose? He doesn't wave it away. The answer is beyond human understanding, he says, because God's knowing is not like ours, and he holds on to both. God knows, and you choose. Readers have argued about that answer. But the sentence about Moses stands either way. Nothing written at your birth closes the road.
screen: `EVERY PERSON CAN TURN EITHER WAY.` · `NOTHING DECREED AT BIRTH.` · `WITHOUT CHOICE, NO RETURN.` · `GOD KNOWS, AND YOU CHOOSE.` · then, large: `YOU CAN BE MOSES.`

segments.voice: Notice the small choices already in this moment: whether to keep sitting, whether to follow a thought or let it go, whether to breathe a little slower. Then think of one moment in your day where you usually run on autopilot, the reply you always give, the scroll you always start, and decide freely what you'd do there instead. If you pray, you can hold the words "therefore choose life" for a breath.
You can be Moses. Maimonides' teaching that every person is free to become righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam, and nothing at birth decides it. Today's word.
Your line: you can be moses. Either road is open, and the choosing is yours. See you tomorrow.

1153.title: The messianic age
1153.hook: Maimonides pictures the world running as usual, but without war or hunger
1153.howItsDone: The traditional daily prayers ask for redemption, and the Aleinu prayer, said near the end of services, looks toward a world united in knowing God. Some communities connect that hope to feeding the hungry and working for peace now.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses or Jeroboam, and nothing at birth decides which. Your line: you can be moses. Today, the picture that closes the whole code.

Sunrise. A baker unlocks the shop. Buses run. Children argue about whose turn it is. Nothing about the morning looks miraculous. And yet nobody anywhere is marching to war, and nobody anywhere goes to bed hungry. That ordinary-looking morning is close to how Maimonides describes the days of the messiah, in the closing chapters of his law code. Not fire from the sky. Not a new set of physics. The same world, with the worst things gone.
screen: `AN ORDINARY MORNING.` → `NO WAR. NO HUNGER.` → `THE SAME WORLD.`

segments.voice: The messianic age. Maimonides closes the Mishneh Torah with it, in the Laws of Kings. First, the world keeps its habits. Don't imagine, he writes, that anything of the world's ordinary order will be canceled, or that something new will enter creation. He quotes a sage in the Talmud: the only difference between this world and the days of the messiah is that Israel will no longer be subject to the rule of other kingdoms. Second, the wolf and the lamb. Isaiah says, "And the wolf shall dwell with the lamb." Maimonides reads it as a parable: nations once fierce as wolves will live in peace. Third, what he doesn't know. How it will all happen, nobody will know until it does. The prophets' words are unclear, and sages disagreed. So he warns readers not to get lost calculating the details. Fourth, what it's for. The sages didn't long for those days to rule the world, or to eat and drink and celebrate, he writes, but to be free to study and to know God, with nothing pressing on them. There will be no famine and no war, no envy and no rivalry. Good things will be plentiful, and the whole world's occupation will be to know God. He ends the entire code with Isaiah: "for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea." Jews hold a range of views on the messiah today, and some streams speak more of a messianic age than a person. This is his picture: ordinary days, made safe.
screen: `THE WORLD KEEPS ITS HABITS.` · `THE WOLF AND THE LAMB, A PARABLE.` · `HOW, NOBODY KNOWS YET.` · `FREE TO KNOW GOD.` · then, large: `AS THE WATERS COVER THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Picture tomorrow morning where you live, your street, your kitchen, the people nearby, and take one thing out of the picture: somebody in your town who is hungry. See the morning without that, and ask plainly what one step this week moves toward it, a bag of groceries, a meal for a neighbor, a small recurring gift. If you pray, you can hold the words "as the waters cover the sea" for a few breaths.

1154.title: The Guide for the Perplexed
1154.hook: written for a student torn between philosophy and faith
1154.howItsDone: Some Jews study the Guide for the Perplexed slowly, chapter by chapter, with a teacher or a study partner, in study halls, universities and adult classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the messianic age: an ordinary morning, with no war and no hunger. Your line: the world, at peace. Today, a new book, written for one torn student.

A student packs his bags and leaves his teacher. He's bright, he loves the Torah, and he's been studying logic, astronomy and philosophy. And the two are pulling him apart. The verses say God walks in a garden, sits on a throne, smells the smoke of an offering. His philosophy says God can't have a body. Does he give up the books, or give up the reasoning? His teacher, far away now, decides to write for him and send the chapters as they're finished. Those chapters became a book.
screen: `A STUDENT LEAVES.` → `TORAH AND PHILOSOPHY PULL APART.` → `HIS TEACHER WRITES.`

segments.voice: Moreh Nevukhim. The Guide for the Perplexed, by Maimonides. First, the student. The book opens with a letter to a student named Joseph. Joseph came to study with him, Maimonides writes, quick and eager, and when they were separated he decided to write for him. Sometimes a book begins as one person worrying about another. Second, the reader. The Guide, he says plainly, is not for beginners or the general public. It is for a faithful, observant person who has also studied philosophy and now finds the plain sense of certain verses troubling. That person is perplexed: follow reason and seem to abandon the Torah, or hold the Torah and feel reason has been thrown away. The book is meant to show a road that keeps both. Third, the method. Much of the opening part goes word by word through terms the Bible uses for God, words like place, standing, seeing, coming down, and shows how each can carry a figurative meaning. Fourth, the warning. He wrote some parts on purpose so that not everything lies on the surface. A reader has to work, compare chapters and pay attention, and he asks readers not to explain the book to others hastily. This is not a book you skim. It's a conversation with a teacher who expects you to think, and over the next days we'll open it a chapter at a time.

1155.title: Human language (Guide 1:26)
1155.hook: the Torah speaks in human language
1155.howItsDone: Jews who study the Guide often read its opening chapters alongside the verses they discuss, asking of each bodily word for God what it figuratively means. The phrase 'the Torah speaks in human language' is also a familiar principle in classical commentary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moreh Nevukhim, a book written for a faithful student torn by philosophy. Your line: for the perplexed. Today, one of its keys.

A four-year-old asks where the sun goes at night. The parent doesn't open with orbits and the turning of the earth. They say something like: the sun goes to sleep on the other side of the world. It isn't a lie. It's the truth, said in words a four-year-old can hold. Later the child will learn more, and the first answer won't feel like a trick. It'll feel like a door that opened on time. A phrase from the rabbis says the Torah does something like this.
screen: `WHERE DOES THE SUN GO?` → `TRUE, IN WORDS A CHILD CAN HOLD.` → `A DOOR THAT OPENS ON TIME.`

segments.voice: Human language. In Hebrew, dibrah Torah kilshon b'nei adam: the Torah speaks in the language of human beings. First, where it starts. The phrase comes from the Talmud, where some rabbis use it in arguments about how to read a verse: don't squeeze a hidden lesson out of every doubled word, because people talk that way. Second, what Maimonides does with it. In chapter twenty-six of the Guide's first part, he gives the phrase a bigger job. The Torah speaks so everyone can understand it, including people who aren't philosophers. And people at large, he says, can only picture something as real if it's a body, something that moves, acts, lives. So the Torah describes God with words like those: God sees, speaks, comes down, is alive. Third, an example. At Babel, the verse says, "And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower." To Maimonides, this isn't a report about travel. It's human words saying that God attends to what people do. Fourth, why it matters. This one phrase lets a reader hold the text with both hands: honoring every word, and still reading the words as speech meant for people. That was the relief the Guide offered the perplexed student. Now look back over this week: a loan or a job, so nobody needs to ask; giving where neither knows; the path of return; you can be Moses; a world at peace; a book for the perplexed; and a Torah that speaks our language.
screen: `A PHRASE FROM THE TALMUD.` · `SPOKEN SO EVERYONE CAN UNDERSTAND.` · `THE LORD CAME DOWN TO SEE.` · `HOLDING THE TEXT WITH BOTH HANDS.` · then, large: `THE TORAH SPEAKS IN HUMAN LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a verse with God's hand, or eyes, or walking, or speaking in it, and say it to yourself slowly. Then ask: if this is a figure of speech, what is it saying in plain terms, care, power, attention? Let the picture stay a picture, and let the meaning come up underneath it.
